data: support and resistance levels supplied to customers by six FX firms
method: tests whether the published levels predict intraday trend interruptions
finding: Strong evidence that the levels help predict intraday trend interruptions, but predictive power varies across exchange rates and firms.
relation: The classic 'levels carry information' result; its benchmark of real versus other levels parallels the random-entry design. Published (firm-supplied) levels, not close-line levels.

data: individual currency stop-loss and take-profit orders (first such data)
finding: Take-profit orders cluster at round numbers and stop-loss orders just beyond them, offering an explanation for reversals at support/resistance and for fast moves after levels are crossed.
relation: Mechanism for 'liquidity at levels' stories; says nothing about net profitability.

method: relation of technical levels to book depth
finding: Support and resistance levels coincide with peaks in depth on the limit order book, and moving-average forecasts reveal where depth sits; technical rules locate depth already in place.
relation: Supports 'levels reflect resting liquidity'; no profit test.

method: heuristic discovery algorithm for support and resistance levels
finding: Discovered levels reverse price trends at a statistically significant rate; levels with more previous bounces are more likely to bounce again, and bounce probability decays as a level ages.
relation: Direct evidence on 'fresh versus tested' levels: more past bounces raise bounce probability, which cuts against 'fresh is best'.

method: criterion to detect supports and resistances; memory-effect test
finding: Memory effects in price dynamics are associated with the detected support/resistance values: prices more likely re-bounce than cross them.
relation: Same direction as Chung and Bellotti on repeated bounces.

data: daily closes, last two decades, adjusted for dividends and splits
method: rule-based identification of horizontal support/resistance levels, tested as trend-reversal predictors and for abnormal returns
finding: Results are described as aligned with the efficient market hypothesis (abstract truncated in this read).
relation: Shows how a codified level definition is validated on stocks.

method: tests with Monte Carlo and comparison indices
finding: The index's rise and fall is restrained at support and resistance levels at multiples of 100, and after breaking a 100-level it moves more than otherwise warranted.
relation: Round-number barrier evidence.

method: profitability of signals from breaking of levels, with transaction costs
finding: Trading-range breaks generate profitable signals even after transaction costs, and signals built from chartists' inputs are more frequent and profitable.
relation: Level-break rules in FX; era and data are old.

data: filter rules supplied by technical analysts
finding: Some profits are available in trending periods but not on average, and the result is strengthened after transaction costs.
